content: Primary prevention of high cholesterol is considered the most effective strategy to reduce the global burden of cardiovascular disease. The National Cholesterol Education Program (NCEP) recommends both population-based and clinical-based approaches for primary prevention. Physicians are advised to set both short-term and long-term goals for their patients, taking into account individual risk factors and the 10-year risk of coronary heart disease (CHD). Therapeutic lifestyle changes and lowering low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol are strongly advocated. Therapeutic lifestyle changes should be recommended to all individuals to mitigate long-term cardiovascular risk. These changes include smoking cessation, dietary modifications, weight management, and increased physical activity. A prior meta-analysis demonstrated that dietary cholesterol reduction was associated with a CHD risk reduction comparable to that achieved with drug therapy. A recent randomized controlled trial by Jenkins et al. showed that cholesterol-lowering diets significantly reduced LDL cholesterol levels and 10-year CHD risk at six months compared to a control diet. The Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) guidelines recommend a multifaceted lifestyle approach to reduce CHD risk, with therapeutic lifestyle changes being a cornerstone of this strategy. If therapeutic lifestyle changes fail to achieve the desired LDL cholesterol goals, drug therapy should be considered. Statins are typically the first-line medications for this purpose. Numerous trials have evaluated the role of statin therapy in primary prevention. A recently published Cochrane meta-analysis, which included 14 randomized controlled trials with 34,272 participants, demonstrated a significant reduction in all-cause mortality, combined fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular disease (CVD) endpoints, and revascularizations with statin therapy in individuals without pre-existing cardiovascular disease. However, heterogeneity in the effects between studies was noted. Another meta-analysis evaluating statins in primary prevention showed significant reductions in major coronary events, major cerebrovascular events, and revascularizations among 42,848 participants, but no significant changes in CHD mortality or overall mortality were observed. The ALLHAT-LLT trial (2002) found no significant difference in CHD mortality between the group treated with pravastatin 40 mg daily and the usual care group, despite well-controlled hypertension and moderately elevated LDL cholesterol levels. Possible explanations for the lack of significant reduction included modest cholesterol reduction, the absence of a placebo group, and a high crossover rate of high-risk subjects. The ASCOT-LLA trial (2003) involved hypertensive patients with total cholesterol levels below 251 mg/dL who were randomly assigned to atorvastatin 10 mg daily. This trial demonstrated a significant reduction in non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), fatal CHD, and stroke (both fatal and non-fatal). However, no significant difference in all-cause mortality was observed. The trial was stopped early due to the beneficial effects of the treatment. The ASPEN trial (2006) included 1,905 patients with diabetes and no prior CHD. The primary composite endpoint and secondary endpoints, including cardiovascular mortality, fatal/non-fatal MI, revascularizations, strokes, or hospitalization for angina, were similar between the treatment group (atorvastatin 10 mg daily) and the placebo group. The JUPITER trial (2008) was a landmark study that randomly assigned 17,802 healthy individuals with LDL cholesterol levels below 2 g/L to receive rosuvastatin 20 mg daily or placebo. This trial demonstrated significant benefits in reducing cardiovascular events, with a maximum follow-up of five years.
